claims.claim: Under U.S. federal tax law, a section 501(c)(3) organization may not qualify for exemption if a substantial part of its activities is attempting to influence legislation, but it may engage in some lobbying without losing exemption; the IRS defines legislation as action by Congress, a state legislature, a local council or similar body on acts and bills, plus public referenda and ballot initiatives, and states that it does not include actions by executive, judicial, or administrative bodies.

The IRS measures lobbying either by the substantial part test, which weighs all pertinent facts and circumstances including time devoted by paid staff and volunteers and expenditures, or by the section 501(h) expenditure test, which organizations other than churches and private foundations may elect by filing Form 5768; under the expenditure test the nontaxable lobbying amount is a sliding scale beginning at 20 percent of the first $500,000 of exempt purpose expenditures and capped at $1,000,000.

For an organization with a section 501(h) election in effect, the grassroots nontaxable amount is 25 percent of the lobbying nontaxable amount, and a 25 percent excise tax is imposed on excess lobbying expenditures; an organization that lobbies excessively over a four-year period may lose exempt status. Under the substantial part test route, an organization that loses exemption for excessive lobbying may also face a 5 percent excise tax under section 4912, with a matching 5 percent tax on managers who knowingly agree to the expenditures; churches and private foundations are not subject to the section 4912 tax.

Section 501(c)(3) organizations are absolutely prohibited from directly or indirectly participating in or intervening in any political campaign on behalf of or in opposition to any candidate for elective public office; nonpartisan voter education, candidate forums, voter registration and get-out-the-vote activity are permitted only if conducted without bias favoring or opposing a candidate, and violation can bring denial or revocation of exemption and excise taxes.

Federal award funds carry restrictions independent of an organization's tax status: 2 CFR 200.450 makes the costs of influencing activities associated with obtaining federal awards unallowable and, for nonprofit organizations and institutions of higher education, makes unallowable the costs of attempting to influence federal or state legislation, of attempting to influence election outcomes, and of legislative liaison activity carried on in knowing preparation for unallowable lobbying, with stated exceptions including technical and factual presentations made in response to a documented request from a legislative body or member, activity specifically authorized by statute, and activities already excepted by the Internal Revenue Code provisions at 26 U.S.C. 501(c)(3), 501(h) and 4911 such as nonpartisan analysis, study, or research.

31 U.S.C. 1352 bars a recipient of a federal contract, grant, loan, or cooperative agreement from expending appropriated funds to pay any person for influencing or attempting to influence an officer or employee of an agency, a Member of Congress, or congressional staff in connection with the awarding, making, extension, continuation, renewal, amendment, or modification of that contract, grant, loan, or cooperative agreement, and requires a written declaration and certification.

Program-specific rules can be stricter than general tax law: under 45 CFR part 1612, Legal Services Corporation recipients may not attempt to influence legislation, may not engage in grassroots lobbying, and may not participate in or attempt to influence any rulemaking, while 45 CFR 1612.5(a) expressly permits administrative representation for an eligible client in a proceeding that adjudicates that client's particular rights or interests.

Rules differ for public employees: under 5 U.S.C. 1502, a covered state or local officer or employee may not use official authority or influence to interfere with or affect the result of an election or nomination, may not coerce another state or local officer or employee into political contributions, and may not be a candidate for elective office if the employee's salary is paid completely, directly or indirectly, by loans or grants made by the United States or a federal agency, subject to listed exceptions; the employee retains the right to vote as chosen and to express opinions on political subjects and candidates.

In Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, decided March 23, 1970, the U.S. Supreme Court held that welfare benefits are a matter of statutory entitlement for qualified persons so that procedural due process applies to their termination, and that an evidentiary hearing is required before termination; the hearing need not be a judicial or quasi-judicial trial, but the recipient must receive timely and adequate notice detailing the reasons, an effective opportunity to confront adverse witnesses and present arguments and evidence orally, the right to retain counsel, a decisionmaker who states the reasons and evidence relied on, and an impartial decisionmaker who did not participate in the determination under review.

Federal Medicaid regulations set out what an appeal right concretely contains: 42 CFR 431.205(d) requires the state hearing system to meet the due process standards of Goldberg v. Kelly; 431.210 requires a notice to state the intended action and effective date, a clear statement of the specific reasons, and the specific regulations that support or the change in law that requires the action; 431.211 requires advance notice at least 10 days before the date of action; 431.221(b)-(d) bars the agency from limiting or interfering with a hearing request, permits the agency to assist, and allows a reasonable time not to exceed 90 days from the mailing of the notice to request a hearing; 431.240(a)(3) requires an impartial official not directly involved in the initial determination; and 431.242 gives the applicant or beneficiary or their representative the opportunity to examine the case file and all documents to be used, before and during the hearing, to bring witnesses, to present argument without undue interference, and to question or refute testimony including cross-examination of adverse witnesses.

Under 42 CFR 431.230, if the agency sent the required advance notice and the beneficiary requests a hearing before the date of action, the agency may not terminate or reduce services until a decision is rendered after the hearing, unless it is determined at the hearing that the sole issue is one of federal or state law or policy and the agency promptly informs the beneficiary in writing; if the agency's action is sustained by the hearing decision, the agency may institute recovery procedures to recoup the cost of services furnished solely by reason of that continuation.

42 CFR 431.222 permits a state agency to respond to a series of individual hearing requests by conducting a single group hearing, permits consolidation only in cases in which the sole issue involved is one of federal or state law or policy, and requires that each person be permitted to present his own case or be represented by an authorized representative.

The phrase 'nothing about us without us' is an expression of the disability rights movement; the health-equity literature that uses it cites James I. Charlton's 1998 book Nothing About Us Without Us: Disability Oppression and Empowerment (University of California Press) as its source in the scholarly record.

Federal Long-Term Care Ombudsman regulations model consent-directed advocacy: under 45 CFR 1324.19(b), regardless of who made the complaint, the Ombudsman or representative of the Office serves the resident, must offer privacy, must discuss the complaint with the resident to determine the resident's perspective, must request the resident's informed consent in order to investigate, must determine the resident's wishes about whether allegations are reported and whether identifying information may be disclosed, must advise the resident of the resident's rights, and must work with the resident to develop a plan of action; 45 CFR 1324.19(a)(5) also directs representatives to review and comment on existing and proposed laws, regulations and policies and to facilitate the ability of the public to comment.

The Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program is authorized under Title VII of the Older Americans Act and operates in all states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and Guam, with a full-time State Long-Term Care Ombudsman directing each statewide program.

Under 5 U.S.C. 553, general notice of proposed rulemaking is published in the Federal Register; the agency must give interested persons an opportunity to participate through submission of written data, views, or arguments; after consideration of the relevant matter presented the agency must incorporate in the adopted rules a concise general statement of their basis and purpose; and 5 U.S.C. 553(e) gives every interested person the right to petition for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of a rule. Section 553(a)(2) states that the section applies except to the extent that a matter relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts is involved.

Civil legal aid is an ally in individual advocacy: the Legal Services Corporation describes itself as the largest funder of civil legal services in the United States, funding nonprofit programs that handle matters including family law and domestic violence protection, veterans' benefits, eviction and foreclosure, employment and reentry, and access to Medicare and Social Security, and notes that people can lose income, housing, or custody without a right to an attorney.

Legal protection for internal advocacy is narrower than students often assume. The National Labor Relations Board describes protected concerted activity as employees acting together to address work-related issues, including an individual acting on the authority of other employees, bringing group complaints to the employer's attention, trying to induce group action, or preparing for group action, with no requirement of union membership. However, 29 U.S.C. 152(2) excludes the United States, any state, and any political subdivision from the definition of 'employer,' and 29 U.S.C. 152(3) excludes supervisors, independent contractors, agricultural laborers, and individuals in domestic service from the definition of 'employee.'

Professional ethical standards require advocacy while acknowledging that it happens inside an employment relationship. The 2024 NOHS Ethical Standards direct human service professionals to be informed about relevant local, state, and federal laws and to advocate for amendments or changes when laws conflict with ethical standards or client rights (Standard 12); to establish processes to identify client needs and assets and facilitate planning and advocacy at individual, community, and societal levels (Standard 15); and to advocate for social justice and systemic change within their workplace, communities, and legislative systems (Standard 16). The same standards direct professionals to honor commitments to employers to the fullest extent possible (Standard 22), to participate in efforts to establish and maintain employment conditions conducive to high quality client services (Standard 23), and, when a conflict arises between responsibility to the employer and responsibility to the client, to work with all involved to manage the conflict (Standard 24).

The NASW Code of Ethics (2021 revision) treats advocacy as a professional obligation to the broader society in section 6, including standards on social welfare, public participation in shaping social policy and institutions, and social and political action to ensure equal access to resources, employment, services and opportunities and to expand choice and opportunity, particularly for people who are vulnerable, disadvantaged, oppressed, or exploited.

The advocacy literature is conceptually fragmented and rarely measured: a 2026 scoping review of 146 documents on advocacy in public health and healthcare found advocacy consistently framed as a deliberate, value-driven practice oriented toward systemic change and equity, but with considerable conceptual and operational variability, and reported that only 6 of the included studies (4 percent) used specific measurement instruments, none of which were standardized.

Controlled outcome evidence for structured advocacy interventions is thin. A 2025 systematic review of experimental studies of medical-legal partnerships addressing health-harming legal needs found only seven eligible studies, of which two were randomized controlled trials each assessed as low risk of bias; all studies reported positive effects on primary endpoints including stress, diabetes, and immunization, and the authors concluded that additional efficacy research is needed given the small number of studies.

Evidence on self-advocacy is encouraging but preliminary: a 2025 mini-review of self-advocacy and self-determination among autistic adolescents and young adults reported encouraging associations with educational and employment outcomes, socialization, relationship and identity development, self-concept, and quality of life, while stating that the literature rests on pilot and correlational studies, that larger and more racially and ethnically diverse samples are needed because existing samples were small and majority White, and that the review itself did not use a systematic search strategy.

positions: Practice and professional literature treats advocacy as an established, effective, and ethically required part of the role.
The measured literature is fragmented, largely conceptual and case-based, uses no standardized outcome instruments, and offers only a handful of experimental studies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the duty and the toolkit as professional practice, and separately reports the evidence as thin and mostly non-experimental. It claims positive effects only where controlled studies exist (a seven-study medical-legal partnership review with two low-risk-of-bias RCTs) and characterizes self-advocacy findings as associational rather than causal. No general effectiveness claim is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How students should read the word 'lobbying'.
positions: Common shorthand treats advocacy as permitted and lobbying as prohibited for nonprofits.

U.S. federal tax law permits 501(c)(3) lobbying within measured limits while prohibiting candidate campaign intervention absolutely, and separate funding rules can restrict activity that is not lobbying at all.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the shorthand is wrong and gives the actual structure: two measurement methods for lobbying limits under tax law, an absolute campaign prohibition, and independent restrictions attached to federal award funds, particular programs, and public employment. It cites the IRS, the Internal Revenue Code, and the Code of Federal Regulations directly and states that it is not legal advice.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether appeal procedure can be taught generically.
positions: Appeal rights are broadly similar across benefit programs.
Deadlines, continuation rules, and hearing procedures are program-specific and set by each program's own statute and regulations.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the federal Medicaid fair hearing regulations as a labeled worked example of what an appeal right can contain, states explicitly that the numbers are Medicaid's and not universal, and directs the reader to the notice and the governing rule in each case.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no verifiable advocacy content at all: it described advocacy only as 'a foundational concept' used to 'organize information' with no reference to case or cause advocacy, self-advocacy, appeals, or the legal boundaries.
The draft's vocabulary entry defined advocacy circularly as 'a foundational Social Work & Human Services concept covered in this lesson.'
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study skills rather than any advocacy content, and cited no sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with researched content built on primary legal sources (IRS guidance, 26 U.S.C. 4911, 31 U.S.C. 1352, 5 U.S.C. 553 and 1502, 29 U.S.C. 152, 2 CFR 200.450, 42 CFR part 431 subpart E, 45 CFR 1324.19, 45 CFR part 1612) and peer-reviewed evidence.
Added the case/cause distinction and the pattern-of-denials bridge, grounded in the group hearing rule at 42 CFR 431.222.
Added self-advocacy with the 'nothing about us without us' attribution to the disability rights movement and to Charlton (1998), and the consent-directed ombudsman model at 45 CFR 1324.19(b).

Added the precise lobbying and campaign-activity boundary demanded by the assignment, distinguishing what is limited from what is absolutely prohibited, and noting the separate federal award, program-specific, and public-employee rules.
Added an explicit statement that the lesson is educational material and not legal advice, and that rules vary by jurisdiction, program, and employer.
Downgraded all effectiveness language to match the scoping review and systematic review findings.

rightsIssues: The NASW Code of Ethics is copyrighted. It is used REFERENCE_ONLY: the lesson describes what section 6 requires in original wording and reproduces no code text.
The NOHS Ethical Standards are used REFERENCE_ONLY. Standard numbers and their subject matter are named and paraphrased; no standard text is reproduced.

IRS web guidance is U.S. federal agency content used here as REFERENCE_ONLY. Facts and figures are restated in original wording; the sliding-scale figures and the 25 percent grassroots and excise-tax figures were independently confirmed against 26 U.S.C. 4911 on uscode.house.gov.

Peer-reviewed sources (Monaci et al. 2026, John et al. 2025, Martino et al. 2025, Gooderham et al. 2026) carry Creative Commons licenses but are used REFERENCE_ONLY: their findings are restated in original prose and none of their wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.notes: Full standards page retrieved and the numbered standards read directly to confirm numbering and content: Standard 12 (duty to be informed about relevant local, state and federal laws and to advocate for amendments or changes when they conflict with ethical standards or client rights); Standard 15 (establish processes to identify client needs and assets, draw attention to them, and facilitate planning and advocacy at individual, community and societal levels); Standard 16 (advocate for social justice, eliminate oppression, raise awareness of systems of discrimination, advocate for systemic change within workplace, communities and legislative systems); Standard 22 (honor commitments to employers to the fullest extent possible); Standard 23 (participate in efforts to establish and maintain employment conditions conducive to high quality client services); Standard 24 (when responsibility to employer conflicts with responsibility to the client, work with all involved to manage the conflict). Paraphrased only. Reused source id; URL matches the existing registry record.

sourceRecords.title: Defining advocacy in public health: a scoping review to inform policy, training, and equity-oriented action
sourceRecords.provider: Monaci M, Korenjak M, Credi B, Bigi S, Barello S; International Journal for Equity in Health 25:71 (2026), BMC, read on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC API. Source for the honest evidence statement: a scoping review across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and CINAHL including 146 documents; advocacy consistently framed as a deliberate, value-driven practice oriented toward systemic change, social justice and equity, but with considerable conceptual and operational variability across clinical care, public health promotion, community mobilization and policy reform; and the finding that only 6 studies (4 percent) reported the use of specific measurement instruments, none of which were standardized. Findings restated in original wording; the no-derivatives license means no adaptation of its text.

sourceRecords.title: Efficacy of Medical-Legal Partnerships to Address Health-Harming Legal Needs: A Systematic Review of Experimental Studies in the Field
sourceRecords.provider: John J, Murphy T, Zientek E, Liaw W, Dimgba O, Nguyen T-A, Burnett C, Aitken M, Sharma S; American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine (2025), SAGE, read on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC API. Source for the claim that controlled evidence on structured advocacy interventions is thin: seven eligible experimental studies; populations largely women, of color, and of lower socioeconomic status; all studies showed positive effects on primary endpoints including stress, diabetes, and immunization; two studies were randomized controlled trials, each with low risk of bias; and the authors' conclusion that additional efficacy research is needed given the small number of studies.

sourceRecords.title: The role of self-advocacy and self-determination in positive adjustment for autistic adolescents and young adults: a mini-review
sourceRecords.provider: Martino DC, Brantley A, Scarpa A; Frontiers in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry 4:1542543 (2025), read on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC API. Source for the modest self-advocacy evidence claim: encouraging associations between self-advocacy and self-determination and educational and employment outcomes, socialization, relationship development, identity development, self-concept and quality of life; and the authors' own stated limitations, that the base consists of pilot and correlational studies needing more robust methodology, that samples were small and majority White so generalization is limited, and that no systematic search strategy was used because the literature is still emerging.

sourceRecords.title: Addressing ableism in healthcare: integrating critical disability theory into health services research
sourceRecords.provider: Gooderham E, Smith J, Lavergne R, McCracken RK, Hedden L; International Journal for Equity in Health 25:504231 (2026), BMC, read on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read via the Europe PMC API. Used narrowly to attribute 'nothing about us without us' to the disability rights movement and to its scholarly source: the review describes the expression as the disability rights movement's, and its reference list cites James I. Charlton, Nothing About Us Without Us: Disability Oppression and Empowerment (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1998). Charlton's book was not read directly; the attribution is reported as it appears in this peer-reviewed source.
